<explanation>
Below is an outline you can use to draw a precise system-architecture diagram for the Python-Cheatsheet project.  It’s a static documentation website with two auxiliary “build” pipelines (one for plots/data, one for PDF/index generation), no dynamic server, all content served as static files (e.g. via GitHub Pages).  

1. Identify the main components  
   - Developer Workstation  
     • Source repository (Markdown README.md, index.html, parse.js, CSS, fonts)  
     • Build scripts:  
       – Python “web” pipeline: convert_table.py, update_plots.py → produces web/covid_cases.js, web/covid_deaths.js, continents.csv etc.  
       – Python “pdf” pipeline: pdf/create_index.py, pdf/remove_links.py → produces pdf/index_for_pdf.html and cleans XML chapters.  
   - Version Control & Hosting  
     • Git/GitHub (push code) → GitHub Pages (serves static files) or any static-file server  
   - Client Browser (Frontend)  
     • index.html + parse.js: reads README.md, builds the cheatsheet DOM in the browser  
     • CSS files (style.css, style_dark*.css) and font assets under web/… for styling  
     • JS modules (covid_cases.js, covid_deaths.js) + plotly.js for interactive graphs  
     • pdf/index_for_pdf.html + XML files under pdf/Acrobat for the printable PDF version  

2. Relationships and data flows  
   - Developer runs Python scripts → updates or generates data files (JS modules, HTML indexes, cleaned XML) → commits to repo  
   - GitHub Pages pulls static content on push → hosts index.html, parse.js, CSS, JS, pdf/, web/ folders  
   - Browser requests index.html → parse.js transforms README.md into HTML UI → loads CSS, fonts and web/*.js → invokes Plotly to render graphs from pre-built data modules  
   - Browser requests pdf/index_for_pdf.html when printing PDF → loads XML chapters and the html index → produces printable view  

3. Architectural patterns / design principles  
   - Static-site architecture (no dynamic backend)  
   - Build pipelines treat Python scripts as “producers” of static assets  
   - Frontend composition: a “parser” script (parse.js) drives content generation at runtime  
   - Clear separation of concerns:  
     • Content (README.md)  
     • Style (CSS + Web fonts)  
     • Client logic (parse.js + plotly)  
     • Data pipelines (Python)  
     • PDF pipeline (Python + XML)  

4. Relevant technologies  
   - Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6), Plotly.js  
   - Build / Data tools: Python 3 (`convert_table.py`, `update_plots.py`, `create_index.py`, `remove_links.py`), CSV, XML  
   - Hosting: GitHub Pages or any static-file server  

5. Guide to tailoring your diagram  
   - Static documentation site focus:  
     • Emphasize no backend server—everything is pre-built or browser-driven  
     • Show “Developer” → “Build Scripts” → “GitHub Pages” → “Browser” flow  
   - Data-pipeline sub-system:  
     • Show Python scripts fetching external COVID/continents data → generating JS modules for client use  
   - PDF sub-system:  
     • Show Python scripts processing XML chapters → producing PDF-friendly HTML index → consumed by browser printer  

6. Diagramming recommendations  
   - Use boxes to represent each component type (Developer tools, Hosting, Browser)  
   - Draw directional arrows for:  
     • Developer → Build Scripts → Repo/Hosting  
     • Browser → Hosting (fetch static files)  
     • parse.js → README.md (content parsing)  
     • Browser → web/*.js → Plotly → render graphs  
   - Use color or shapes to distinguish:  
     • Build-time components (Python scripts) in one color  
     • Hosting layer in another  
     • Runtime components (Browser + parse.js + CSS + JS) in a third  
   - Label external services (e.g. “fetch CSV from owid-covid-data.csv”) as cloud icons  

7. Detail level  
   - Include each top-level directory as a sub-component (root, web/, pdf/)  
   - Show the key files under each (README.md, index.html, parse.js; web/*.js, style.css; pdf/*.py, Acrobat/*.xml)  
   - Annotate interactions (e.g. “parse.js reads README.md at runtime”, “update_plots.py writes covid_cases.js”)  

By following this structure and these guidelines, you’ll capture all essential architectural elements of the Python-Cheatsheet project in a clear, accurate system-design diagram.  
</explanation>
